title: Tattoo License Requirements by State
summary: A plain guide to tattoo licensing in Florida, Texas, New York City and California: who issues it, what it costs and how long it takes.
body_markdown:
Most US states require a license or registration before you can legally tattoo, but not all of them, and no two work the same way. There is no national tattoo license. Rules are set at state level, and in some states at county or city level, which means the requirements change the moment you cross a line on a map.


The differences are bigger than most artists expect. Florida licenses you as an artist for 60 dollars a year. Texas does not license artists at all, it licenses the studio you work in. New York City licenses artists but not shops. California has no state license, you register with the county you work in.


This guide covers Florida, Texas, New York and California first, because they carry the most working artists. The remaining states follow.


## Do you legally need a license to tattoo?


In most states, yes. But the thing being licensed is not always you.


Three models exist across the four states covered here:


- The state licenses the artist. Florida and New York City work this way. You apply, you pay, you hold a license in your own name.
- The state licenses the business, not the artist. Texas works this way. There is no Texas tattoo artist license to apply for. The studio holds the license and you are named on its application.
- The county licenses the artist. California works this way. You register with the local health agency for the county you work in, not with the state.


Working without the license your state requires is a criminal offense, not a fine. In Florida, tattooing anywhere other than a licensed establishment is a second-degree misdemeanor under Florida Statutes 381.00785. In Texas, operating outside the rules is a Class A misdemeanor and each day counts as a separate offense under Health and Safety Code 146.018. In California, performing body art without registering is a misdemeanor under Health and Safety Code 119323.


## What is usually required


The specifics vary, but the same components come up across states:


- Being 18 or older. This is consistent across all four states covered here.
- Bloodborne pathogen training. Required in Florida, California and New York City. The length and the renewal cycle differ, and some states will only accept a course from their own approved provider list.
- A passing exam score, where the state attaches an exam to the training.
- Working at a licensed establishment. Florida, Texas and California all require the location to be permitted, separately from anything you hold.
- An application fee and a renewal cycle, usually annual.


One thing that is widely assumed and is not required in any of these four states: a formal apprenticeship with a set number of hours. Florida states it plainly. Its licensing FAQ says an apprenticeship is not required to apply for a tattoo artist license. Apprenticeships remain the normal way artists learn, and individual studios will expect one. They are simply not a legal condition of licensure in these states.


## Requirements by state

New York appears twice because the state and the city run separate systems. See the New York section below.


## Florida


Florida runs the most conventional system of the four. You hold a license in your own name, it costs 60 dollars, and it is renewed every year.


- Issued by: Florida Department of Health, administered through county health departments.
- Required: a tattoo artist license. Florida Statutes 381.00775 states a person may not tattoo the body of any human being in this state unless the person is licensed as a tattoo artist or registered as a guest tattoo artist.
- Minimum age: 18.
- Training: a Department-approved bloodborne pathogen and communicable diseases course, minimum three hours, specific to the tattoo industry. Florida publishes an approved provider list.
- Exam: attached to the course. Minimum 50 questions, 70 percent to pass, under rule 64E-28.006.
- Fee: 60 dollars, renewed annually at 60 dollars. A lapsed license costs 85 dollars to reactivate, which is the 60 dollar renewal plus a 25 dollar reactivation fee.
- Establishment: a separate Tattoo Establishment License at 200 dollars, valid for one location and non-transferable.
- No apprenticeship required.


Two Florida details that catch artists out. The license runs for one year from the date it was issued, not on a fixed calendar cycle, so the expiry date is personal to you. And the application will not be processed until you name the licensed establishment you work at or intend to work at, which means you cannot get licensed in the abstract before you have somewhere to work.


A license is also required if you do not charge, and for students or apprentices tattooing other people as part of their training.


## Texas


Texas is the one most commonly written up incorrectly. There is no Texas tattoo artist license. Searching for one will not find it, because it does not exist.


- Issued by: Texas Department of State Health Services.
- What is licensed: the studio, per location. The only license types DSHS issues are Tattoo Studio, Body Piercing Studio and Temporary Event.
- Artists: named on the studio's license application under rule 25 TAC 229.403, not licensed individually.
- Training: no hours and no approved course list. Rule 25 TAC 229.405(i) requires each artist to have the education, training and experience, or any combination of those, to practice aseptic technique and prevent the transmission of bloodborne pathogens. That is a competence standard with no set syllabus.
- Exam: none found in the statute, the rules or on DSHS pages.
- Studio fee: 927 dollars on the DSHS fee schedule for both initial and renewal, plus a 100 dollar late fee.
- Location: a studio must be in a permanent, non-dwelling building, separated from living quarters floor to ceiling with no access between them.


This does not mean Texas is unregulated for artists. You still have to meet the competence standard, be named on a licensed studio's application, and work somewhere licensed. What you do not do is hold a personal license.


One change to watch. Texas now requires human trafficking prevention training for each employee of a tattoo studio under Health and Safety Code 146.0075. The Health and Human Services Commission adopted its implementing rule, 26 TAC 370.1, effective 11 October 2026. DSHS says the approved courses will be listed on its site and that at least one will be free. Check with DSHS for the deadline that applies to you.


## New York


New York is two systems, and which one applies depends on whether you are inside New York City.


### New York State, outside New York City


Public Health Law Article 4-A says a permit is required. Section 461 states that no person shall be a body piercing specialist or tattooist, and no business shall operate a tattoo studio, without first obtaining a permit from the department.


That permit is not currently being issued. The New York State Department of Health states on its own body art page that statewide health regulations for tattooing and body piercing are currently being developed, and that until the new regulations are in place, local regulations, if any, apply.


So an artist working in Buffalo or Albany is governed by their county or city health department, not by Albany. There is no state fee, no state training standard and no state application to complete. Check with the local health department for the county you work in.


### New York City


New York City runs a complete and well-documented system of its own.


- Issued by: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, processed through the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.
- Required: a Tattoo License. You need one to work as a tattoo artist in New York City.
- Minimum age: 18.
- Training: the DOHMH Health Academy Infection Control Course, followed immediately by a written exam.
- Fee: 100 dollars for two years, or 126 dollars if you apply online, which covers both the license and the course. An online convenience fee of 2 percent applies.
- Renewal: every two years at 100 dollars.
- Shops: New York City licenses artists, not parlors. There is no NYC shop permit from DOHMH.


Worth knowing: the license covers microblading, permanent makeup, scalp pigmentation and micro-needling, so cosmetic practitioners need the same license. You cannot start working until the physical license and photo ID badge arrive, which takes four to six weeks. And NYC requires your advertising to carry the words licensed by the New York City Department of Health along with your license number.


## California


California has no statewide tattoo license and no state licensing board. The Safe Body Art Act sets minimum standards, and each county or city health agency runs registration itself.


- Issued by: the local health agency for the county, city, or city and county where you work.
- Required: practitioner registration. Health and Safety Code 119306 states a person shall not perform body art if he or she is not registered with the local enforcement agency.
- Minimum age: 18.
- Training: a bloodborne pathogen exposure control course specific to your practice, minimum two hours, completed before you register, plus a two-hour update every year. The trainer has to be approved by your local enforcement agency, so a course accepted in one county may not be accepted in the next.
- Also required: evidence of hepatitis B vaccination, proof of immunity, or a signed declination.
- Exam: no state practitioner exam.
- Fee: set locally. Los Angeles County was 54 dollars at last check, and other counties differ. Check your county's current fee schedule.
- Renewal: annual, by a process each local agency sets.
- Facility: a separate health permit, also local. Each county sets its own fee, so check your county's current schedule.


The thing that catches people moving to California: there is no reciprocity and no transfer. A license from another state does not carry over, and neither does a registration from another California county beyond a short grace period. You register again, with a locally approved course, in the county where you will actually work.


## Guest spots, conventions and tattooing across state lines


This is where artists get caught, because the rules that govern a two-day guest spot are not the rules that govern the shop you are guesting at. Every state covered here handles it differently, and one combination traps people completely.


### The Texas problem


Florida offers a Guest Tattoo Artist Registration at 35 dollars, valid for up to 14 consecutive days. It is the cheap, fast route for a visiting artist, and it is the obvious thing to reach for.


It is only open to artists who already hold an active tattoo artist license, registration or certification from another jurisdiction. Florida states that if your state does not require a tattoo artist license registration or certification, you must apply for a Florida tattoo artist license.


Texas does not license artists. So a Texas-based artist booking a weekend guest spot in Miami cannot use the 35 dollar guest registration. They need the full Florida artist license at 60 dollars, plus the approved bloodborne pathogen course, plus the exam, plus a named licensed establishment on the application. That is weeks of lead time for a two-day booking, and it is invisible until you read both states' rules side by side.


The same logic applies anywhere a guest route requires a home license you do not have.


### What each state offers a visiting artist


- Florida: Guest Tattoo Artist Registration, 35 dollars, up to 14 consecutive days. Requires a license from your home jurisdiction. Rule 64E-28.004 says to file at least 14 days before you practice.
- New York City: Temporary Tattoo Artist License, 50 dollars, valid seven days, cannot be renewed or extended. You must show proof you are licensed elsewhere, work under a licensed NYC artist, and supply a notarized letter from them. You cannot work independently on it.
- California: your county registration is valid in other California jurisdictions for no more than five consecutive days, or 15 days total, in any one calendar year. Beyond that you register in that county too.
- Texas: there is no guest artist permit, because there is no artist license. Events of seven days or less need a Temporary Tattoo Studio license, which the event holds rather than you.


Conventions add a second layer. In Florida the event needs its own Temporary Tattoo Establishment License at 200 dollars, and every artist working it still needs their own license or guest registration. In California, the county hosting the event sets the temporary booth permit rules and fees, so ask that county's health agency before you book.


## How much does a tattoo license cost?


For the artist, between nothing and 100 dollars across these four states, because the cost sits in different places depending on the model.


- Florida: 60 dollars a year.
- New York City: 100 dollars for two years, or 126 dollars applying online including the course.
- California: set by county. Los Angeles County was 54 dollars a year at last check.
- Texas: nothing, because there is no artist license. The 927 dollar cost sits with the studio.


Training is the cost people forget to budget for, and in California it recurs every year rather than once.


## How long does it take to get licensed?


Plan in weeks, not days. The training course and exam have to be completed before you apply, not alongside. New York City then mails the license and photo ID badge, which takes four to six weeks, and you cannot work until both arrive. Florida wants the establishment named before it will process you. Florida's guest registration asks for 14 days notice.


If you are booking a guest spot or a convention, start the paperwork the month before, not the week before.


## Frequently asked questions


### Do you need a license to tattoo?


In most states yes, but what gets licensed varies. Florida and New York City license the artist. Texas licenses the studio and has no artist license at all. California requires you to register with your county rather than the state. Check your own state, and if you work in California, your own county.


### Is it illegal to tattoo without a license?


Where a license is required, yes, and it is usually a criminal offense rather than a fine. Florida treats tattooing outside a licensed establishment as a second-degree misdemeanor. Texas treats violations as a Class A misdemeanor with each day a separate offense. California treats performing body art without registration as a misdemeanor.


### Do you need an apprenticeship to get a tattoo license?


Not in any of the four states covered here. Florida states directly that an apprenticeship is not required to apply. Apprenticeships are still how most artists learn and most studios will expect one, but they are not a legal requirement for licensure in these states.


### How much is a tattoo license?


60 dollars a year in Florida. 100 dollars for two years in New York City. Los Angeles County was 54 dollars a year at last check, with other California counties setting their own. Nothing in Texas, where the studio pays 927 dollars instead.


### Does a tattoo license transfer between states?


No. There is no reciprocity between states. Some states offer a short-term guest route, but it usually requires you to hold a license at home, and it is capped at days rather than months.


### Do you need a separate license for the shop?


Usually, and it is separate from anything you hold. Florida charges 200 dollars for an establishment license and Texas 927 dollars for a studio. California counties set their own facility permit fees. New York City is the exception, licensing artists but not parlors.


### Can you tattoo from home?


Not in Florida, Texas or California unless the space is separately permitted as a facility in its own right, with its own entrance and no internal door to the living space. Florida states plainly that a license does not allow you to tattoo at a customer's home.


## Once you are licensed, what to set up next


Licensing gets you legal. It does not get you booked.


The practical next steps are the ones that turn a license into work: somewhere clients can see your availability and book without a back-and-forth in your DMs, a booking form that collects what you need before the appointment, a deposit policy that holds, and clear terms clients agree to when they book.


Venue handles that side. It is free to start, with no monthly fee.


Last verified October 2026. Licensing rules change, so this page is re-verified every six months.
